13107-001.name_en: Memorial to the Ishiwara-cho victims of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake fire
13107-001.summary_en: The fires that followed the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 reduced most of the city to ashes; Honjo and Fukagawa wards suffered worst, and countless lives were lost. Of about 8,000 residents of Ishiwara-cho in Honjo Ward, about 7,000 burned to death. The stone was relocated in 1931.

13107-004.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake fire
13107-004.summary_en: The Honjo area suffered enormous damage in the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923. A memorial to the victims was erected in March 1931; because it was damaged during the air raid on Tokyo of 10 March 1945, the present stone was rebuilt in 1961.

13107-005.name_en: Stone Jizo statue for the Tatekawa riverbank victims of the 1923 earthquake fire
13107-005.summary_en: On the afternoon of 1 September 1923, the day of the Great Kanto Earthquake, several hundred people on the Tatekawa riverbank, trapped by black smoke and fierce flames, threw themselves into the river, and many drowned; many others burned to death. The Jizo was erected in November 1924, and its base inscription dedicates it to these victims.

13107-006.name_en: Grave of those killed in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
13107-006.summary_en: Probably erected for victims of the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 in the Ryogoku police district. Its inscriptions give the date, “ninety-odd” dead and the donor, the Aioi Barbers' Association, and record a gift of 50 yen to the temple for memorial services.

13107-007.name_en: Memorial to those crushed to death in the 1855 Ansei Edo earthquake
13107-007.summary_en: Around 10 pm on 11 November 1855 a great earthquake struck Edo, and tens of thousands of people were crushed or burned to death. According to the inscription, a group of plasterers from Azabu planned this memorial to ease the victims' suffering, and the high priest of Zojoji, praising their aim, wrote the invocation “Namu Amida Butsu” for it.

13107-008.name_en: Memorial to those killed in the two Ansei disasters of 1855 and 1856
13107-008.disaster_en: Ansei Edo earthquake (11 Nov 1855) and Ansei Edo typhoon (23 Sep 1856)
13107-008.summary_en: The Ansei Edo earthquake of 11 November 1855 brought down houses and storehouses and started fires in dozens of places; on 23 September 1856 a typhoon flattened houses and riverside floods swept others away. Many were crushed, burned or drowned. Carved with six Jizo figures, the memorial was set up in 1857 for the dead of both disasters.

13107-009.name_en: Memorial to all who died in the 1855 Ansei Edo earthquake and its fires
13107-009.summary_en: Erected jointly in 1866 by residents of the Kumamoto Shinden domain's lower residence in Honjo and of Nakanogo Takecho for those who died in the earthquake and fires. The front bears the invocation “Namu Amida Butsu” written by Ekoin's 17th head priest. A Meiji-era plan of the temple grounds shows it as the “Ansei earthquake mound”.

13107-011.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1783 Mount Asama eruption in Shinshu and Joshu
13107-011.disaster_en: Tenmei eruption of Mount Asama (4 Aug 1783)
13107-011.summary_en: The front inscription dedicates the memorial to those killed by the great eruption of Mount Asama in 1783. Inscriptions on the other three faces say that a confraternity of morning worshippers, led by eight organisers, built it with offerings they had saved.

13107-010.name_en: Memorial to those killed in the disasters since the 1783 Mount Asama eruption
13107-010.disaster_en: Tenmei eruption of Mount Asama (4 Aug 1783) and later disasters
13107-010.summary_en: In 1789 the shogun Tokugawa Ienari ordered six leading temples to hold services for those killed in the repeated disasters since the 1783 Asama eruption. Ekoin held its service in 1789 and erected this memorial, whose inscription recounts the eruption, years of famine and epidemics in Tohoku and Kanto, and the great Kyoto fire of 1788.

13107-002.name_en: Memorial to Aioi Police Station officers who died on duty in the 1923 earthquake fire
13107-002.summary_en: In the fires after the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, 34 officers of the Aioi Police Station, led by their chief, died trying to rescue people fleeing the flames. The stone was erected on 1 September 1933; beside it stands a memorial to Honjo Haraniwa Police Station officers who died on duty. Both were moved here in 2013.

13101-003.name_en: Monument to the neighborhood defended from fire in 1923
13101-003.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, which killed more than 100,000 people, was the largest natural disaster in Japan's history, and fire destroyed more than 200,000 houses. This neighborhood escaped because its residents worked together for hours after the quake to put out fires and stop them spreading.

13102-001.name_en: Memorial to those who found refuge at Shin-Ohashi Bridge in 1923
13102-001.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake struck at 11:58 am on 1 September 1923, as families were cooking lunch; fires from kitchen stoves and charcoal braziers spread quickly in strong winds. While many bridges over the Sumida River burned and fell, the steel Shin-Ohashi Bridge of the time survived largely undamaged and saved many people fleeing the fires.

13104-001.name_en: Memorial to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
13104-001.summary_en: In the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, the former Yotsuya Ward had 168 people killed or injured and 500 houses burned. Proposed by newspaper companies in the ward, the memorial was built with the support of 103 backers, including the ward assembly, neighborhood associations and trade associations. Its title was written by the then head priest of Zojoji.

13101-001.name_en: Monument on the site of the Imperial College of Engineering (Kobu Daigakko)
13101-001.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, with more than 100,000 dead and more than 300,000 buildings destroyed or burned, was the largest natural disaster in Japan's history. The former Imperial College of Engineering building here collapsed; the Ministry of Education and the Board of Audit were built in its place. The monument is made from its bricks.

13104-002.name_en: Mizukake Jizo statues and memorial to the dead of the 1923 earthquake and fire
13104-002.summary_en: In the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 the former Ushigome Ward had 105 people killed or injured and 926 houses wholly or partly destroyed, but almost no fires, so it took in many evacuees. The memorial to the dead was erected the next year; the two standing Jizo statues came from the Gobyo Bridge on Mount Koya.

13103-002.name_en: Statue of Sho Kannon in memory of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
13103-002.summary_en: Fires broke out in many places after the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, reducing the Shimbashi, Atago and Hamamatsucho areas to ashes. In Shiba Ward, now part of Minato Ward, nearly half of all households were burned out, and the dead were cremated here at Densoin temple.

13101-004.name_en: Monument where Emperor Showa stood to view the city's reconstruction in 1930
13101-004.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 killed more than 100,000 people, and there were even rumours that the capital would be moved. In 1930, two days before the reconstruction celebrations, Emperor Showa stopped here first while inspecting the rebuilt downtown districts; Tokyo Bay could then be seen from this spot. The stone was rebuilt in 1989 after weathering.

13102-003.name_en: Memorial for the tenth anniversary of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
13102-003.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake, at 11:58 am on 1 September 1923, left 99,331 dead and 43,476 missing, with 128,226 houses destroyed and 447,128 burned. The slogan carved on the monument, “For the sudden earthquake, constant readiness”, urges people to remember the day and never let such a disaster happen again.

14100-001.name_en: Monument to the reconstruction after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
14100-001.summary_en: In the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, the former city of Yokohama had 28,169 buildings completely destroyed and 26,623 people killed. Yokohama Park, where the monument stands, served as a refuge for many of the city's residents during the disaster.

14201-003.name_en: Memorial to the refuge at Suwa Shrine after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
14201-003.summary_en: After the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, the number of people sheltering at Suwa Shrine reached 400 by 5 September, and some lived at the shrine for a while. The monument was put up by the evacuees themselves.

14201-002.name_en: Memorial to the Yokosuka victims of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
14201-002.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 was a disaster without precedent. Yokosuka did not escape: there were scenes of devastation everywhere, and 517 people in the city died. The memorial was moved to this site in 1936; nearby are a stone listing the victims' names and a Jizo statue dedicated to them.

14201-004.name_en: Memorial to the 1923 earthquake dead who washed ashore at Mabori
14201-004.summary_en: In the days and weeks after the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, around 10 bodies, thought to be victims from Tokyo and Yokohama, washed ashore on the Mabori coast of Yokosuka and were buried here. The memorial was erected in 1930, seven years after the disaster.

14201-001.name_en: Memorial tower to the victims of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake in Uraga
14201-001.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 caused slope collapses and fires in Uraga. In Nishi-Uraga, Mount Atago collapsed, burying 74 houses and about 100 people, and at Dokkuhara a slide buried 7 passers-by alive. The former town of Uraga alone lost 202 people. Rebuilt after the war, the tower honours victims of the earthquake and of shipwrecks.

14204-001.name_en: Memorial to the nine people killed in the 1903 Zaimokuza landslide
14204-001.summary_en: On 2 October 1903 heavy rain set off a slope collapse in the former Zaimokuza district, engulfing 2 houses and killing 9 residents. Two of them were pupils of Yuigahama Elementary School (now Kamakura Daiichi Elementary School).

14208-001.name_en: Monument recording the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake at Myokoji temple
14208-001.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 left the temple's main hall and living quarters half-destroyed and brought down its Shichimen Hall, bell tower and other buildings. The former town of Zushi, where the stone stands, had 794 buildings destroyed and 76 people killed.

14301-001.name_en: Monument to the completion of the rebuilt Hayama boat basin
14301-001.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923 raised the coastline and left the boat basin of Hayama Port unusable. Fishing boats had to be moored on the beach instead, and many were wrecked in bad weather. The monument commemorates the rebuilding of the boat basin.

14205-007.name_en: Memorial to the 1923 Great Kanto and 1924 Tanzawa earthquakes
14205-007.disaster_en: Great Kanto Earthquake (1 Sep 1923) and Tanzawa earthquake (15 Jan 1924)
14205-007.summary_en: The Great Kanto Earthquake, at 11:58 am on 1 September 1923, left 33 dead and 52 injured in the former village of Kawaguchi, with 180 houses destroyed, 269 half-destroyed and 5 burned down. The Tanzawa earthquake of 15 January 1924 caused further damage.

14205-006.name_en: “Alas, 1 September”: memorial to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
14205-006.summary_en: In the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923, most houses in the former town of Fujisawa collapsed and 116 people died.

26100-001.name_en: Statue of the bond between teachers and pupils, for the 1934 Muroto Typhoon victims
26100-001.summary_en: On 21 September 1934 the winds of the Muroto Typhoon, which raged across western Japan, brought down wooden buildings at several schools in and around Kyoto, killing 162 children and 4 teachers trapped beneath them. The present statue was rebuilt after the war.

26100-010.name_en: Stone record of the 1934 Muroto Typhoon damage at Yosei school
26100-010.summary_en: When the Muroto Typhoon struck the Kinki region on 21 September 1934, Yosei Elementary School recorded 3 wooden classrooms destroyed, 3 half-destroyed, 4 tilted and 15 needing repair, and the roof of its indoor gymnasium badly damaged. None of the children was hurt.

26100-006.name_en: Memorial tower for the Junna school victims of the 1934 Muroto Typhoon
26100-006.summary_en: On 21 September 1934 the winds of the Muroto Typhoon trapped more than 200 people under the collapsed building of Junna Elementary School (now Saiin Elementary School). Erected on the first anniversary, the tower bears the names of the 32 children and the teacher, Matsuura, who died.

26100-002.name_en: Memorial stone recording the 1935 flood inundation
26100-002.summary_en: Before dawn on 29 June 1935, after days of heavy rain, all the rivers in Kyoto overflowed and more than 40,000 houses in the city were flooded. In the Ogawa district the Kamidachiuri-Ogawa stone bridge fell at 5 am, and houses along the stream collapsed, were swept away or were half-destroyed. The inscription records water four shaku (about 1.2 m) deep.

26100-007.name_en: Memorial to the 1934 Muroto Typhoon disaster at Junna school
26100-007.summary_en: On 21 September 1934 the winds of the Muroto Typhoon, which raged across western Japan, trapped more than 200 people under the collapsed building of Junna Elementary School (now Saiin Elementary School); 32 children and a teacher, Matsuura, were killed.

26100-004.name_en: Memorial to the 41 pupils of Nishijin school killed by the 1934 Muroto Typhoon
26100-004.summary_en: On 21 September 1934 the winds of the Muroto Typhoon, which raged across western Japan, brought down a building of Nishijin Elementary School, and 41 children trapped beneath it died.

27100-007.name_en: Flood defense monument recalling the storm surges of 1934, 1950 and 1961
27100-007.disaster_en: Muroto Typhoon (21 Sep 1934), Typhoon Jane (3 Sep 1950) and Second Muroto Typhoon (16 Sep 1961)
27100-007.summary_en: Nishi Ward in Osaka has been flooded again and again by storm surges brought by typhoons. Many lives and much property were lost: in Osaka City, 990 people died in the Muroto Typhoon of 1934, 211 in Typhoon Jane of 1950 and 6 in the Second Muroto Typhoon of 1961.

27100-001.name_en: Stone recording the 1854 Ansei earthquake and tsunami at the two river mouths
27100-001.disaster_en: Ansei Tokai earthquake (23 Dec 1854) and Ansei Nankai earthquake (24 Dec 1854)
27100-001.summary_en: After the Ansei Nankai earthquake of 24 December 1854, a tsunami struck people who had taken refuge in boats moored on the Aji, Kizu and other rivers, with heavy losses. The stone was erected as a warning to later generations, because the lesson of a similar disaster in the 1707 Hoei earthquake had not been heeded.

27100-008.name_en: Stone record of the 1934 Muroto Typhoon storm and flood in Kujo
27100-008.summary_en: The Muroto Typhoon hit Osaka at about 8 am on 21 September 1934 with winds of 60 m per second and a storm surge of nearly 3 m. The city's dead and missing reached 990; 28 wooden school buildings collapsed and 269 pupils died. In Kujo, roof tiles flew like leaves and every house was flooded above floor level.

27100-002.name_en: Monument to the 1854 Ansei earthquake and tsunami
27100-002.disaster_en: Ansei Tokai earthquake (23 Dec 1854) and Ansei Nankai earthquake (24 Dec 1854)
27100-002.summary_en: People who took to small boats to escape the earthquakes of 23 and 24 December 1854 were swept upstream, boats and all, by a tsunami that surged into the mouth of the Kizu River, and a great many died. The inscription warns that a rumbling sea or disturbed tides are signs of a tsunami, and that people should evacuate.

28100-001.name_en: Monument for Remembrance and Reconstruction, with the 1.17 Light of Hope
28100-001.summary_en: The Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake of 17 January 1995 left 6,437 people dead or missing. The monument keeps the disaster in memory, passes on the story of the recovery, honours the victims, encourages citizens and speaks for the value of worldwide solidarity in recovering from major disasters.

28100-002.name_en: Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park
28100-002.summary_en: A 60 m stretch of Meriken Wharf, badly damaged in the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake of 1995, is preserved as it was left. The park shows how the Port of Kobe was damaged and rebuilt, and hands down the lessons of the earthquake, the importance of the port and the joint effort that restored it.

28100-024.name_en: Monument to Kano-cho's recovery from the 1938 Hanshin flood
28100-024.summary_en: Days of summer rain peaked in a downpour on 5 July 1938, setting off debris flows across Mount Rokko and flooding rivers all at once. Torrents from the Nunobiki valley and nearby streams tore into Kano-cho, killing 12 people and damaging over 220 houses. The monument was moved here in March 2007 from 200 m to the north-east.

28100-003.name_en: Kobe Earthquake Reconstruction Memorial Park (Minatonomori Park)
28100-003.summary_en: The park was created as a symbol to nurture the spirit of the aid and volunteers that came from across Japan and the world after the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake of 1995. Its guiding idea is to watch Kobe move from recovery to growth as its trees grow.

28100-025.name_en: “Flowing Stones” monument to the 1938 Hanshin flood
28100-025.summary_en: The downpour of 5 July 1938 set off debris flows across Mount Rokko; the Uji and Kusudani rivers in Kusudani-cho overflowed, sweeping away about 150 houses and killing more than 10 people. Made of boulders from the flood, the monument records the damage and notes that, as everyone joined in the recovery, its name may be read “sasuga” (“truly admirable”).

28100-026.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 1938 Hanshin flood
28100-026.summary_en: The downpour of 5 July 1938 set off debris flows across Mount Rokko, and rivers overflowed all at once. Arata-cho was swept by muddy torrents in an instant, with 125 victims and about 1,800 houses flooded.

28100-027.name_en: Memorial tower to the victims of the 1938 Hanshin flood
28100-027.summary_en: The downpour of 5 July 1938 set off debris flows across Mount Rokko, rivers overflowed all at once, and vast amounts of earth and sand buried Kobe. The tower stands where the Ishii and Tennodani rivers meet, where damage was especially severe, to hand down the vow that such a disaster must never happen again.

28100-008.name_en: Requiem monument to the victims of the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake
28100-008.summary_en: The monument stands in the pond around the west building of the Disaster Reduction and Human Renovation Institution, built so that the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake is not forgotten. Shaped like clock hands at 5:46, when the quake struck, it holds a register of every victim. The Kobe Wall and part of a Hanshin Expressway pier are also on the site.

28100-010.name_en: Memorial to those who died in the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake
28100-010.summary_en: At 5:46 am on 17 January 1995, with a great rumbling of the ground, a powerful earthquake struck directly beneath the Hanshin-Awaji region. It brought down 143,331 houses and killed 5,502 people, in what became known as the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake.

28100-009.name_en: Monument of Life (Inochi no Hi) for the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake
28100-009.summary_en: The Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake, at 5:46 am on 17 January 1995, killed 100 people in the Kawaike area, which covers Egeyama-cho, Oi-dori, Matsumoto-dori and Kamisawa-dori.

34100-012.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the landslide of June 1965
34100-012.summary_en: Erected in a corner of a park at the foot of Hijiyama hill to honor those who died in a landslide on 20 June 1965.

34100-007.name_en: Monument honouring Segawa Uichi for the recovery from the 1926 and 1928 floods
34100-007.summary_en: The inscription records the causes and damage of the floods and debris flows brought by torrential rain in 1926 and 1928, and the work of Segawa, head of Yamamoto village at the time, in the recovery.

34302-001.name_en: Memorial to the 1926 flood of the Enokawa and other rivers
34302-001.summary_en: Torrential rain on 11 September 1926 flooded the Enokawa and other rivers. Embankments broke along about 6.4 km and more than 20 bridges were washed away; 3 people died, 26 houses were swept away and 101 were half-destroyed.

34100-014.name_en: Monument to the 2014 Hiroshima landslide disaster
34100-014.disaster_en: Heavy rain of August 2014 (Hiroshima landslides, 20 Aug 2014)
34100-014.summary_en: A red line carved on the monument marks the height of 62 cm above the ground reached by the debris flow of 20 August 2014, passing on to future generations what happened in the disaster.

34100-003.name_en: Monument to the flood and debris flows of September 1926
34100-003.summary_en: The inscription, in classical Chinese, describes the flood and debris flows caused by torrential rain on 11 September 1926 and the damage they did.

42201-007.name_en: Memorial tower to the 1982 Nagasaki flood at the site of Shianbashi bridge
42201-007.disaster_en: Heavy rain of July 1982 (Nagasaki flood, 23 Jul 1982)
42201-007.summary_en: In the torrential rain of 23 July 1982 the water here, at the site of Shianbashi bridge, reached 1.57 m, and people, cars and everything else disappeared beneath the muddy flood. Residents rebuilt, and the district regained its liveliness. The tower is topped by a red-seal trading ship sailing towards the future, in praise of that spirit of recovery.

42201-005.name_en: Monument to recovery from the 1982 Nagasaki flood and to friendship with China
42201-005.disaster_en: Heavy rain of July 1982 (Nagasaki flood, 23 Jul 1982)
42201-005.summary_en: On 23 July 1982 torrential rain left 262 people dead or missing in Nagasaki; of the stone bridges on the Nakashima River, 6 were washed away and 3 half-destroyed. The monument was made in China, which helped build the river's stone bridges; it shows a Chinese boy and a Japanese girl together taming a dragon that brings wind and rain.

42201-002.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1982 Nagasaki flood in Narutaki
42201-002.disaster_en: Heavy rain of July 1982 (Nagasaki flood, 23 Jul 1982)
42201-002.summary_en: Shortly after 5 pm on 23 July 1982 a violent thundery downpour of around 100 mm struck, and a massive debris flow in the Narutaki area left 23 people dead and 1 missing. The memorial honours them and passes on the lesson so that such a disaster is never repeated.

35305-004.name_en: Monument to the 1893 flood of the Migama River
35305-004.summary_en: On 14 October 1893, after five days of rain, Mount Monju collapsed and the Migama River overflowed. The flood killed 23 people and swept away 16 houses in the former village of Kamano.

35305-003.name_en: Memorial to the 110 people killed in the 1886 Gonotsubo flood
35305-003.summary_en: Heavy rain every day from about 20 September 1886 set off a landslide that blocked the Kubo River and formed a natural dam. At 5 pm on the 24th the dam burst, and the debris flow killed 110 people in Gonotsubo and buried 62 houses.

35305-001.name_en: Monument to the 1886 Gonotsubo flood disaster
35305-001.summary_en: Heavy rain every day from about 20 September 1886 set off a landslide that blocked the Kubo River. At 5 pm on the 24th the natural dam burst, and the debris flow killed 110 people in Gonotsubo and buried 62 houses. The inscription notes that the mountain had also collapsed in 1333 and that preventive measures are needed.

30205-004.name_en: Flood-level marker for the 1953 Kishu flood
30205-004.summary_en: The heavy rain of 18 July 1953 broke the embankments; the torrent destroyed hundreds of houses in an instant and laid waste more than 600 hectares of farmland. The marker records the flood level so that the disaster is not forgotten, though it has been moved since it was set up and may no longer show the true level.

30381-001.name_en: Stone record of the 1854 Ansei Nankai tsunami
30381-001.summary_en: The Ansei Nankai earthquake of 24 December 1854 brought a tsunami to Mihama, and people who fled onto the river in boats were sunk by it. The inscription teaches that great earthquakes bring tsunamis and that people should take refuge on the higher ground of the great pine grove.

30205-006.name_en: Monument of Murata Yoshinari, recalling the 1889 Hidaka River flood
30205-006.summary_en: Heavy rain on 19–20 August 1889 broke the embankments of the Hidaka River, and the torrent swept away many houses, people and livestock. The flood is said to have killed 219 people.

30205-001.name_en: Monument to the 1953 Kishu flood in Gobo
30205-001.summary_en: Heavy rain of up to 600 mm on 18 July 1953 made the Hidaka River overflow. Across Gobo City 26 people died, 100 went missing and about 3,000 were injured; an estimated 4,000 houses were flooded above floor level, 365 of them swept away, and recovery took several years. The monument urges future generations never to lose their wariness of nature.

30205-007.name_en: Monument to the restoration of Fujii's farmland after the 1953 Kishu flood
30205-007.summary_en: Heavy rain that had fallen since the night before struck all of Kishu on 18 July 1953, hitting the Arida and Hidaka river basins hardest. Landslides filled valleys, embankments broke, torrents swept away people and houses, and farmland was badly devastated. The monument first stood by the prefectural road at Fujii and now stands on the Gobo–Miyama road at Yoshida.

47209-001.name_en: Monument to the 1960 Chile tsunami at Oura
47209-001.summary_en: In May 1960 a magnitude 8.5 earthquake in Chile set off a great tsunami that crossed the Pacific to the seas around Japan. It struck here several times, reaching up to 5 m, destroying Oura Bridge and breaking the seawall.

47209-002.name_en: Site of the 1960 Chile tsunami disaster at Makiya
47209-002.summary_en: On 23 May 1960 a magnitude 8.5 earthquake off Chile set off a great tsunami that crossed the Pacific. Makiya Elementary School stood here, and all of its buildings were destroyed by the tsunami; 3 people died in the area.

47209-003.name_en: History of Yagaji Bridge, washed away by the 1960 Chile tsunami
47209-003.summary_en: The first Yagaji Bridge, completed in 1953, was washed away only seven years later by the 1960 tsunami from an earthquake in Chile, almost on the opposite side of the globe.

47215-001.name_en: Memorial tower to those lost at sea, prompted by Typhoon Iris of 1951
47215-001.summary_en: On 9 May 1951 Typhoon Iris veered towards Okinawa Island and many fishing boats, warned of the storm only after sailing on the 8th, were lost; 41 of 55 people died. The Ou district built the tower in 1956 for those lost at sea and for safe voyages. It is surrounded by sea: take care in typhoons and storm surges.

01423-001.name_en: Monument of gratitude for the Yubari River flood-control works
01423-001.disaster_en: Floods of 7 Sep 1898 and Aug–Sep 1932, and others
01423-001.summary_en: The Yubari River caused severe disasters, including the floods of 1898 and August 1932. Flood-control works begun in 1920 and completed in 1936 turned the area into a town where people can enjoy the water in peace. The monument thanks those who carried out the works; beside it stands another honouring their achievement.

01202-001.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1973 torrential rain in Minamikayabe
01202-001.summary_en: Torrential rain fell on the southern Oshima Peninsula from the night of 23 September 1973 into the 24th. In the former town of Minamikayabe (now northern Hakodate) a record 383 mm caused floods, debris flows and slope collapses; the national highway was cut, 16 houses were destroyed, 8 people died and 11 were injured.

40344-001.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 1973 flood in Satani
40344-001.summary_en: Before dawn on 31 July 1973 torrential rain dropped 239 mm on Sue in just two hours. In the Satani district, debris flows and other damage killed 2 people, destroyed 21 houses and half-destroyed 6, flooded 31, and washed away or buried 23.8 hectares of farmland.

40130-001.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 2005 Fukuoka earthquake (Katsuma)
40130-001.disaster_en: Earthquake west off Fukuoka Prefecture (20 Mar 2005)
40130-001.summary_en: On 20 March 2005 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake centred in the Genkai Sea off Fukuoka City, with a seismic intensity of 6 lower on the Japanese scale, closed roads with slope collapses and damaged houses.

40130-002.name_en: Monument to Genkai Island's recovery from the 2005 Fukuoka earthquake
40130-002.disaster_en: Earthquake west off Fukuoka Prefecture (20 Mar 2005)
40130-002.summary_en: On 20 March 2005 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake centred in the Genkai Sea off Fukuoka City, with a seismic intensity of 6 lower on the Japanese scale, devastated Genkai Island: 19 people were injured and 214 homes damaged, 107 of them completely destroyed.

17361-002.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 1964 Tsubata River flood
17361-002.summary_en: Torrential rain in July 1964 made the Tsubata River overflow, killing 3 people and flooding more than 2,500 houses in all. Repairs and a thorough improvement of the river were completed in 1969, and the monument was erected to mark the recovery.

17211-002.name_en: Memorial to the 1896 Tedori River flood at Yamada
17211-002.summary_en: On the morning of 3 August 1896, after rain from the previous day, the Tedori River embankments broke everywhere. In Yamada 2 houses were swept away, every house was flooded and most fields were lost, but a bamboo-covered embankment (jibushin) held back the torrent so homes were not fully submerged. The stone warns: “Beside a river, floods are hard to avoid.”

17211-003.name_en: Memorial boulders left by the 1896 flood
17211-003.summary_en: The flood of 2–3 August 1896 was “seven parts mud to three parts water”: rice fields became a riverbed of gravel, roads were buried in mud and houses were crushed. Three large boulders the flood carried here were placed in the shrine grounds as memorial stones.

19430-006.name_en: Monument of the Lake Kawaguchi Flood Control Association
19430-006.disaster_en: High water on Lake Kawaguchi (Aug 1983) and the Fuji Five Lakes (9–12 Sep 1991)
19430-006.summary_en: Lake Kawaguchi has no outflowing river, so rising water has long threatened lakeside life. After heavy rain from Typhoon No. 5 in August 1983 the lake kept rising for about a week, flooding hotels and homes near the shore (68 houses above floor level). In September 1991 heavy rain raised the Fuji Five Lakes, submerging lakeside roads and flooding 13 houses.

19424-001.name_en: Memorial to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the floods that followed
19424-001.disaster_en: Great Kanto Earthquake (1 Sep 1923) and the heavy rain that followed (14 Sep 1923)
19424-001.summary_en: The earthquake of 1 September 1923 brought down 72 shrines, temples and houses in Uchino, cracked roads and fields and sent muddy water gushing up; aftershocks were frequent. Heavy rain from the night of 13 September then caused landslides and floods that left trees and stones piled about 2 m deep, ruined the fields and flooded 291 houses.

04100-005.name_en: History of Arahama: Arahama district community monument
04100-005.summary_en: In the Great East Japan Earthquake of 11 March 2011, Sendai's Wakabayashi Ward recorded a seismic intensity of 6 lower. The tsunami that arrived about an hour later flooded 56% of the ward and many people died. Most buildings here were swept away, and the district's residents moved inland in a group relocation for disaster prevention.

04100-006.name_en: Arahama Bell of Memory: Arahama district community monument
04100-006.summary_en: In the Great East Japan Earthquake of 11 March 2011, Sendai's Wakabayashi Ward recorded a seismic intensity of 6 lower, and the tsunami that arrived about an hour later flooded 56% of the ward, killing many people. The distance from the stone pillar to the sphere in front of it is 13.7 m, the greatest height the tsunami reached at Arahama.

04100-001.name_en: “Anew from Here”: Shinhama district community monument
04100-001.summary_en: In the Great East Japan Earthquake of 11 March 2011, Sendai's Miyagino Ward recorded a seismic intensity of 6 upper. The tsunami that arrived about an hour later devastated the city's eastern coast and flooded 35% of the ward. In the historic Shinhama district, known for its white sand and green pines, 58 people lost their lives.

21604-001.name_en: Site of Kaerikumo Castle, buried by the 1586 Tensho earthquake (explanatory stone)
21604-001.summary_en: On the night of 18 January 1586 a huge earthquake struck a wide area of the Tokai, Hokuriku and Kinki regions. A massive collapse of Mount Kaerikumo, where shaking is estimated at intensity 6, is said to have instantly buried Kaerikumo Castle across the Sho River, its town of about 300 houses, over 500 people and even cattle and horses.

10211-002.name_en: Memorial to the 50 people killed in the 1950 Kumanodaira landslide
10211-002.summary_en: On 8 June 1950 a landslide hit Kumanodaira Station on the former Shin'etsu Main Line. During repairs at 6:30 am the next day, a larger landslide killed 50 people: national railway staff and workers, and family members at the staff quarters. The memorial is a statue of a mother found holding her baby. It was moved here in 1968.

10211-001.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1910 landslide and flash flood
10211-001.summary_en: On 10 August 1910, after days of rain, a landslide near today's Onga Bridge blocked the river and formed a natural dam. While people downstream were evacuating, the dam burst and a flash flood swept through the area below, taking 17 lives.

09206-002.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1662 Inari River flood
09206-002.summary_en: In July 1662 heavy rain caused great floods on the Daiya and Inari rivers, and landslides upstream wrought havoc downstream. Huge boulders from Mount Akanagi swept away the town of Inari-machi on the Inari River, east of the Nikko shrine and temple precinct, in a disaster said to have killed more than 140 people.

09206-001.name_en: Sabo tower, a monument to erosion control on Nikko's rivers
09206-001.disaster_en: Floods and debris flows (1902 and earlier)
09206-001.summary_en: Nikko's rivers have suffered great floods and debris flows again and again: in the 820s, in 1532–1534, on the Inari River in 1662 and, more recently, in the Ashio Typhoon of 1902. Each time, many local people died and fields and bridges were lost.

09206-010.name_en: Memorial to the 1949 Imaichi earthquake (Yamakubo district)
09206-010.summary_en: At 8:18 am on 26 December 1949 the Imaichi earthquake struck, causing heavy damage in the two towns and nine villages of the area. Slopes collapsed, the ground cracked, houses tilted and lives were lost, but fortunately no fires broke out. The shrine here was also badly damaged.

09206-011.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 1949 Imaichi earthquake
09206-011.summary_en: At 8:17 am on 26 December 1949 strong shaking struck without warning. Slopes collapsed, the ground cracked and houses tilted or fell, causing severe damage; the shrine that stood here was also damaged.

09206-006.name_en: Memorial to the 1949 Imaichi earthquake (Imaichi district)
09206-006.summary_en: At 8:18 am on 26 December 1949 strong shaking struck the two towns and nine villages centred on the former town of Imaichi. Slopes collapsed, the ground cracked, wells ran dry, houses tilted or fell and lives were lost, but thanks to the townspeople's cooperation no fires broke out.

02207-002.name_en: Memorial to the 1933 Showa Sanriku earthquake and tsunami
02207-002.summary_en: A great earthquake struck at 2:30 am on 3 March 1933. After a loud roar from far out at sea, a great tsunami swept in and took many lives and much property in moments. The monument urges people never to forget the disaster and to stay alert: “Earthquake, a roaring sea — watch out, tsunami!”

02207-001.name_en: Tsunami monument to the 1933 and 2011 tsunamis in Misawa
02207-001.disaster_en: Showa Sanriku earthquake (3 Mar 1933) and Great East Japan Earthquake (11 Mar 2011)
02207-001.summary_en: On 11 March 2011 the Great East Japan Earthquake sent a tsunami more than 7 m high into Misawa, killing 2 people and seriously damaging 188 houses. The monument combines a memorial to that disaster with the inscription moved from the memorial to the Showa Sanriku earthquake and tsunami of 3 March 1933.

02207-003.name_en: “Testament to the Tsunami”: memorial to the 2011 tsunami in Misawa
02207-003.summary_en: On 11 March 2011 the Great East Japan Earthquake sent a tsunami over 7 m high onto the Misawa coast, devastating the fishing port; 2 people died, 1 was injured and 188 buildings were damaged, 96 of them destroyed. To pass on the horror of the disaster, the Misawa East Rotary Club erected this monument and gave it to the city.

42202-001.name_en: Monument to the recovery from the 1967 Sasebo flood
42202-001.summary_en: On 9 July 1967 light morning rain turned at about 11 am into a torrential downpour, recording 225 mm in little more than half an hour. River banks burst, fields were buried and slopes collapsed at more than 40 places. The monument is built of boulders washed down by the flooding Ono River and another local river.

35208-003.name_en: Memorial to the 1942 Suonada Typhoon storm and flood
35208-003.summary_en: The Suonada Typhoon (Typhoon No. 16) struck the Iwakuni area on 27 August 1942, the first great disaster here since the land was reclaimed in 1809. All three embankments were breached, and seawater rose to the top of the stone steps of the local shrine and temple. Of 213 houses, 151 were flooded and 35 swept away, and 23 people died.

34211-001.name_en: Jizo statue in memory of the 17 victims of the 1945 Makurazaki Typhoon
34211-001.summary_en: The Makurazaki Typhoon struck Japan on 17 September 1945, soon after the end of the war, when weather information was scarce and disaster preparedness inadequate, and it caused great damage in many places. Here in Kino, a landslide swallowed 12 houses and took 17 lives.

13205-001.name_en: Memorial tower to the hailstorm of May 1927
13205-001.summary_en: During a thunderstorm on 15 May 1927, hailstones 1.5–2 cm across fell hard for about 30 minutes. Hail rolling off roofs piled 45–60 cm deep under the eaves, and crops such as mulberry, tea and wheat were almost wiped out; damage was worst between Shinmachi, east of Kabe Station, and Ozaku Station. The tower was moved here in 1989.

13205-003.name_en: Monument to the Mizukubo drainage works
13205-003.summary_en: Surrounded by higher ground, this area has long been flooded in prolonged rain, with heavy damage. In the great flood of August 1910 about 100,000 square meters of fields and a dozen or so houses were flooded, and the water was 3 m deep in the city center. Another flood followed in August 1928. The monument has been moved twice.

13209-001.name_en: Torii gate toppled by the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, kept as a memorial
13209-001.summary_en: The earthquake struck at 11:58 am on 1 September 1923, on the day a newly donated torii gate was being unveiled. Many people had gathered in the shrine grounds, but no one was injured. The torii brought down by the quake has been kept as a monument to pass the story on.

34202-009.summary_en: The Geiyo earthquake at 3:27 pm on 24 March 2001 badly damaged Tainomiya Shrine in Nishimitsuta-machi, Kure: its torii gate collapsed, and roof tiles and the stone guardian dogs (komainu) fell.

34202-002.name_en: Memorial to the Miyahara victims of the 1945 typhoon and 1967 heavy rain
34202-002.disaster_en: Makurazaki Typhoon (17 Sep 1945) and heavy rain of July 1967 (9 Jul 1967)
34202-002.summary_en: The Makurazaki Typhoon of 17 September 1945 killed 1,154 people in the then city of Kure and swept away 1,162 houses; 309 of the dead were in Miyahara. On 9 July 1967 torrential rain along the rainy-season front caused landslides and floods across the city, killing 88 people in Kure, 14 of them in Miyahara.

34202-023.name_en: Record of the July 2018 heavy-rain disaster: Yoshiura 1
34202-023.disaster_en: Heavy rain of July 2018 (western Japan floods)
34202-023.summary_en: In the heavy rain of July 2018, debris flows and slope collapses at many points in the Yoshiura district destroyed buildings and cut roads, and 3 people died in this part of Yoshiura.

22219-001.name_en: Tsunami mound for the 1854 Ansei Tokai tsunami in Shimoda
22219-001.summary_en: The Ansei Tokai earthquake and tsunami of 23 December 1854 destroyed or washed away 841 houses in Shimoda, about 98% of the town. Deaths were relatively few, 122 of 3,907 inhabitants (about 3.0%): records show that many people expected a tsunami after the quake and escaped to high ground.

43100-004.name_en: Memorial to the victims of the 1792 Shimabara tsunami
43100-004.disaster_en: Collapse of Mount Mayuyama and tsunami (21 May 1792)
43100-004.summary_en: On the night of 21 May 1792, during volcanic activity at Unzen, an earthquake caused Mount Mayuyama at Shimabara to collapse, sending a great tsunami along the Ariake Sea coast. In this disaster, called “Shimabara's catastrophe, Higo's trouble”, the Uto, Akita and Tamana districts of the Kumamoto domain lost over 4,000 people drowned, 2,000 hectares of fields and over 2,200 houses.

44202-001.summary_en: On the 13th day of the ninth month of 1729 (old lunar calendar), violent winds and flooding crushed more than 20 houses along the boundary between Beppu and Minami-Ishigaki villages, and 21 men and women drowned.
